nameStory: The name 'obesa' comes from Latin meaning 'fat' or 'plump,' referring to this spider's notably thick, robust abdomen compared to other sac spiders. While we don't have a widely-used common name for this particular species, it belongs to the leafcurling sac spider group, named for their habit of building silken retreats in curled leaves.
description: Clubiona obesa is a medium-sized sac spider with a characteristically plump, rounded abdomen that gives it a well-fed appearance. Like other sac spiders, it has a relatively flat body profile and builds silken retreats rather than catching webs. These spiders are typically pale yellow to light brown in color and are active hunters that roam at night. With only one confirmed observation in New England, this species appears to be quite rare in our region.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Notably thick, swollen abdomen that feels firm to the touch if handled - much rounder and plumper than the typically slender abdomens of most sac spiders

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized spider with legs that span about the width of a nickel, body length roughly the size of a small pea

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally pale yellow to light brown coloration with a smooth, almost waxy-looking texture on the abdomen

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: No catching web - instead builds a small, white silken retreat that feels papery and is often tucked into curled leaves or bark crevices

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Active nighttime hunter that moves with quick, darting motions when disturbed, often retreating rapidly to its silken hideout

habitat: Likely found in wooded areas with deciduous trees where it can build retreats in curled leaves, bark crevices, or under loose tree bark. Given its extreme rarity in New England, it may prefer specific microhabitats or be at the northern edge of its range here.

seasonality.spring: Adults may become active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter retreats to hunt and potentially mate.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be encountered hunting at night or found in their silken retreats during the day.
seasonality.fall: May continue hunting into early fall before seeking protected overwintering sites under bark or in leaf litter.
seasonality.winter: Likely inactive, sheltering in protected locations like deep bark crevices or under fallen logs until spring warmth returns.

funFact: This spider is so rarely encountered in New England that there's only been one confirmed sighting - making it potentially rarer to spot than some endangered birds in the region!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other pale sac spiders in the Clubiona genus, but the distinctly swollen, plump abdomen is the key distinguishing feature - think of it as the 'well-fed' member of the sac spider family.
contextualKnowledge: Sac spiders get their name from the silken 'sacs' or retreats they build for shelter, which are different from the sticky webs most people associate with spiders. These retreats serve as both daytime hideouts and nurseries for their eggs.
compareHints: Clubiona obesa stands out from its relatives like the Canada Sac Spider and Riparian Sac Spider by its notably thick, swollen abdomen - while other Clubiona species have more typical slender abdomens. The 'obesa' (fat) in its name is quite literal when compared side-by-side with other leafcurling sac spiders. Its extreme rarity in New England also sets it apart from more commonly encountered relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Clubiona spiralis is most similar to other Clubiona species like the Canada Sac Spider and Riparian Sac Spider, sharing the same general pale coloration and body proportions.
Unlike the Canada Sac Spider which prefers drier woodland habitats, the riparian sac spider sticks close to water sources.
Compared to its inland relatives like the Canada sac spider or riparian sac spider, the maritime sac spider is distinguished primarily by its coastal habitat preference.
Among its Clubiona relatives in New England, the Kaston Sac Spider is most similar to the Canada Sac Spider but tends to be slightly smaller and paler.
Bishop's Sac Spider differs from its more common relatives like the Canada Sac Spider and Riparian Sac Spider primarily in its rarity and subtle coloration differences.
Compared to other Clubiona species in New England, the Canada Sac Spider tends to favor slightly drier woodland habitats than the Riparian Sac Spider, which prefers areas near water sources.
